ch01.note: Linjiang xian (“The Immortal by the River”) is a fixed ci lyric-pattern, whose set metrical form a poet fills with new words. Each of the five parts of this book opens with such a lyric by the author, folded in here as an epigraph at the head of the part’s first chapter. Both the tune-title line and the part-title, “High Ambitions, Admiring Mulan,” turn on the author’s adopted name: Mulan (慕兰) means “admiring [Hua] Mulan,” the legendary woman warrior who took her father’s place in the army (see the note in Chapter 2). The second stanza’s “grand assembly” is a Women’s Day (8 March) gathering of the Northern Expedition years.

Tan Sitong (1865–1898), a reformer from Liuyang and a schoolmate of the author’s father, was one of the “Six Gentlemen” beheaded at Caishikou in Beijing on 28 September 1898 after the failure of the Hundred Days’ Reform; with his fellow townsman Tang Caichang he is remembered as one of the “Two Heroes of Liuyang.” The execution-eve quatrain quoted later in this chapter invokes the Han-dynasty figures Zhang Jian and Du Gen. Corroborated by standard reference works.

The Autumn Harvest Uprising broke out on 9 September 1927 in the Hunan–Jiangxi border area; Wenjiashi, in Liuyang, is where its columns rallied on 19 September—the famous “Wenjiashi turn,” at which Mao Zedong resolved to lead the forces into the countryside rather than assault Changsha. The memoir places the uprising at Wenjiashi; more exactly, Wenjiashi was its rally and turning point. Corroborated with this qualification.

The author’s birth and school name was thus Huang Zhangding (黄彰定), style name Shuyi. She took the name Mulan (慕兰) in 1926 on joining the revolution (Chapter 3), and the name Dinghui (定慧) later, in 1932; in later life, and in this book’s photograph captions, she is generally called Huang Dinghui. On the birth date: the memoir’s own chronology and Chinese biographies give 18 July 1907, while some English sources give 9 July 1906, a discrepancy arising from Chinese age-reckoning. This edition follows the book.

Qiu Jin (1875–1907), a woman revolutionary and feminist who studied in Japan and joined the anti-Qing movement, was executed at Shaoxing on 15 July 1907. The author invokes her repeatedly as a model, and offers her father’s reverence for Qiu Jin as one reason he supported his daughter’s turn to revolution. Corroborated.

ch02.note: Zhu Jianfan (1883–1932), a progressive educator, founded the school that became the Zhounan Girls’ School in Changsha in 1905, selling family property to endow it. Its alumnae include the pioneers of the women’s movement named here—Xiang Jingyu and Cai Chang—as well as Yang Kaihui and the writer Ding Ling. Corroborated.

The name the author adopted, Mulan (慕兰), means literally “admiring Mulan”—an homage to Hua Mulan of the “Ballad of Mulan,” who went to war in her father’s place and served twelve years without her sex being discovered. The pun by which mu (慕, “to admire”) echoes the mu of Hua Mulan (木兰) cannot be reproduced in English. Her birth name was Huang Zhangding (see the note in Chapter 1).
“The Whole River Red” (Man jiang hong) is a celebrated patriotic ci traditionally attributed to the Southern Song general Yue Fei (1103–1142), long a byword for loyal resistance against invaders.

ch03.note: Wan Xiyan (1903–1928), an early Communist and editor-in-chief of the Hankou Republican Daily, became the author’s first husband at Wuhan. Sent afterward to Jiangxi as a provincial Party leader, he was killed there in 1928, in his mid-twenties. Corroborated.

At this point the reissue reproduces a group photograph on which the author, in 1966, inscribed a lyric to the tune Linjiang xian (“The Immortal by the River”): “Forty years ago, this very day—the high tide, joyously met, at Wuhan. How many then were so bold and free? We raised the anti-imperialist banner; talking and laughing, all were heroes. To make a revolution succeed is truly not easy—through hardship and setback, borne with composure! The red flag, fixed forever, streams in the east wind. Keep youth’s vigor ever green; high spirits, in old age firmer still.” An accompanying editorial note records that when she inscribed these lines she was still under political supervision, yet firmly believed herself innocent—a steadfast revolutionary. The photograph and its inscription are given here in a note so as not to break the sentence they interrupt in the source.

The source sentence breaks off here: after “因为我思想” (“because my thinking…”) the clause is left unfinished, and the text passes to the concluding reflection that follows. The account of Qu Qiubai’s persuasion, and the author’s decision to give up the Soviet trip and return to Wuhan, is taken up at the start of Chapter 4. Rendered as it stands, with the break left visible rather than smoothed over.

ch04.anchor: recovering the British concessions at Hankou and Jiujiang
ch04.note: In the wake of mass agitation at Hankou over the killing of Chinese by British marines, the Wuhan Nationalist government’s foreign minister Eugene Chen (陈友仁) negotiated with the British chargé O’Malley the two “Chen–O’Malley agreements,” signed 19 February 1927 (Hankou) and 20 February 1927 (Jiujiang), by which Britain surrendered both concessions—the first time China recovered a foreign concession by negotiation. Crowds had physically occupied the concessions in early January; the formal accords followed in late February. The substance of the memoir’s account is corroborated, though its “9 February” runs about ten days ahead of the signed agreements.

ch04.anchor: On 12 April he suddenly launched a counter-revolutionary coup in Shanghai
ch04.note: The “April Twelfth Incident” of 1927: Chiang Kai-shek, having entered Shanghai, turned on his Communist allies, and with the help of the Green Gang disarmed and massacred the worker pickets and Communists, breaking the first Kuomintang–Communist united front. Chiang set up a rival Nationalist government at Nanjing; the Wuhan government, still in alliance with the Communists, expelled him on 17 April. Corroborated.

ch04.anchor: If it profits the country, I will give my life
ch04.note: A famous couplet by the Qing official Lin Zexu (林则廨, 1785–1850)—the commissioner whose destruction of British opium at Canton in 1839 precipitated the First Opium War—written in 1842 on his way into exile: “若利国家生死以，娴因祸福避趋之” (“If it profits the country, I will give my life; how should I, for fortune or misfortune, flee or seek it?”). Long a byword for selfless public duty.

ch05.anchor: to take no part in the preparations connected with the armed uprising
ch05.note: At this point the source carries its one editorial endnote (the only note original to the chapters in this edition), citing the Huangmei County Gazetteer, p. 215: on 28 July 1927 the Front Committee leading the Nanchang Uprising sent Liu Bocheng, Nie Rongzhen, and the Jiangxi provincial standing-committee members Wan Xiyan and Huang Dao to a secret joint meeting on the armed uprising; by Party decision Chen Tanqiu, Wan Xiyan, and others did not openly take part, but after the insurgent army moved south carried on the underground struggle at Nanchang, Wan Xiyan writing a tract on the conduct of secret work; in February 1928 he left for a special-committee post in southern Jiangxi, was arrested when that organ was broken up, and was killed on 4 April 1928 at Weifuli within the city of Ganzhou. This gazetteer date and place differ from the memoir’s own statement below that he fell in May 1928 assaulting the county town of Wan’an. Modern scholarship (Southeast University’s archives; the martyrs’ registry) supports the gazetteer’s account—arrest and execution at Ganzhou in early April 1928; the memoir’s May/Wan’an version is uncorroborated. Both are left standing here, as in the source.

ch05.anchor: the August Seventh Conference held in Hankou
ch05.note: The emergency conference of the Chinese Communist Party Central of 7 August 1927, held secretly at Hankou, ended Chen Duxiu’s leadership and his “Right-opportunist” line, set the course of armed uprising and agrarian revolution, and was where Mao Zedong offered his dictum that “political power grows out of the barrel of a gun.” Corroborated.

ch05.anchor: the League provincial secretary-general was Rao Shushi
ch05.note: Rao Shushi (饼潟石, 1903–1975), here a Communist Youth League organizer in Jiangxi, later rose to lead the Party’s East China Bureau. In 1954 he and Gao Gang were condemned in the “Gao–Rao anti-Party alliance,” the first great purge of the People’s Republic; he died in prison. The friction the author records here is written with that later history in view. Corroborated.

ch06.anchor: I again ran into Comrade He Chang
ch06.note: He Chang (贺昌, 1906–1935), of Lishi in Shanxi, an early leader of the Communist Youth League and of the Party’s labor and military work, became the author’s second husband. He was killed in 1935 in southern Jiangxi while covering the rearguard after the main Red Army had set out on the Long March. Corroborated.

ch06.anchor: Xiang Zhongfa was nominally the number-one figure
ch06.note: Xiang Zhongfa (向忠发, 1880–1931), a former Wuhan dockers’ leader, was made general secretary of the Party in 1928 as a worker figurehead while Zhou Enlai and others directed the real work, as the author says. Arrested in Shanghai in June 1931, he gave himself up to the Kuomintang and was executed. Corroborated.

Shen Jianlong (沈剑龙) was the son of Shen Dingyi (沈定一, 1883–1928), a landlord-turned-revolutionary and early Communist. When Yang Zhihua left him to marry Qu Qiubai, the three published a joint newspaper notice of the change and remained on good terms—the model of “noble friendship” Zhou Enlai holds up to the author here. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: the Japanese-owned Naigai Wata No. 13 Mill
ch07.note: Naigai Wata (内外棉, Naigaiwata Kaisha) was the largest Japanese-owned cotton-spinning concern in Shanghai, running many numbered mills. It was the killing of the worker-organizer Gu Zhenghong at a Naigai Wata mill on 15 May 1925 that helped ignite the May Thirtieth Movement, which the author invokes later in this chapter. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: Comrade Peng Pai too was unfortunately arrested
ch07.note: Peng Pai (彭湛, 1896–1929), a landlord’s son from Haifeng in Guangdong, founded one of China’s first peasant associations and led the Hailufeng peasant movement and its short-lived soviet—hence the ‘King of the Peasants.’ Betrayed and arrested in Shanghai in August 1929, he was shot at Longhua on 30 August 1929. The prison letters the author describes are preserved in the Collected Works of Peng Pai. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: the detention house of the Longhua Garrison Command
ch07.note: The Longhua Garrison Command, in the southern outskirts of Shanghai, held the Kuomintang’s military prison and execution ground, where many Communists were shot—Peng Pai in 1929 and the ‘Five Martyrs,’ among them the writer Rou Shi, in February 1931. The site is today the Longhua Martyrs’ Cemetery. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: Xiyan's cousin Wan Xixian died of injustice at just this time
ch08.note: The source carries its own endnote here, which reads: ‘Wan Xixian once served as a member of the second Special Committee of the Hunan–Jiangxi border region of the CCP. See Selected Works of Mao Zedong, vol. 1, “The Struggle in the Jinggang Mountains,” the section “Problems of Party Organization” (four-volume edition, p. 76).’ Wan Xixian (宛希先, d. 1930), a native of Huangmei in Hubei, a cousin of the author’s first husband Wan Xiyan and an early leader on the Jinggangshan, was wrongly killed in the over-extended ‘elimination of counter-revolutionaries’ around 1930 and later posthumously rehabilitated. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: which was the program of action for the second
ch08.note: The ‘Li Lisan line’ was the ultra-‘Left’ policy of mid-1930, set out in the resolution the author here carries, which held that a nationwide revolutionary high tide was imminent and ordered armed uprisings and general strikes to seize power in the major cities. The resulting insurrections failed, and the line was corrected at the Third Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee in September 1930. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: In her book My Father Deng Xiaoping, Maomao gives a detailed account
ch08.note: ‘Maomao’ is Deng Rong (邓榱), Deng Xiaoping’s daughter, whose memoir My Father Deng Xiaoping is a standard source. Passing through Hong Kong in late 1929, Deng went on to Guangxi to lead the Baise Uprising (December 1929) and the Longzhou Uprising (February 1930), which founded the Seventh and Eighth Red Armies. Corroborated.

ch08.anchor: Comrades Guan Xiangying and Ren Bishi, who had formerly worked with He Chang
ch08.note: Guan Xiangying (关向应, 1902–1946), a Manchu from Jin County in Liaoning and an early Communist Youth League leader, was secretary of the Party’s Military Commission when he was arrested in Shanghai in 1931. His identity stayed hidden and he was freed some months later—the rescue that opens the next chapter—and he later became a leading Red Army political commissar. Corroborated.

ch09.anchor: to serve as head of the rescue department of the Mutual Aid General Association
ch09.note: The chapter’s title in the source, 营救部长, names this post—‘head of the Rescue Department’ of the Mutual Aid General Association, to which the author is appointed here—rather than meaning ‘to rescue a minister.’ The Rescue Department had its own staff, as the author notes below.

ch09.anchor: was Tan Yankai, military governor and governor of Hunan Province
ch09.note: Tan Yankai (谭延顕, 1880–1930), a Hunan native and Qing metropolitan graduate, governed Hunan three times and became a leading figure of the Nationalist government, serving as the first president of its Executive Yuan. As the author notes, he signed the Wuhan government’s 17 April 1927 order expelling Chiang Kai-shek; the two were later reconciled. Corroborated.

ch09.anchor: Rumor among the common folk had it that the Qianlong Emperor was in fact a Han Chinese
ch09.note: The Chen family of Haining produced high officials for generations under the Qing. A durable folk legend—dramatized in fiction, notably Jin Yong’s The Book and the Sword—held that the Qianlong Emperor was secretly a Han Chinese, a son of this Chen family exchanged at birth for a Manchu girl. Historians reject it, and the author is right to call it untrue. Corroborated as legend only.
